text: An AMI is the template, not the instance. It bundles a snapshot of the root volume — the operating system plus whatever software is already installed on it — launch permissions, and a block device mapping. Pick an image ID in run-instances, and you're telling AWS to build that instance's root volume from this exact template, not configuring one from scratch.

AWS publishes a large catalog of ready-made, patched AMIs for Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, and Windows Server — the normal starting point. You can also build your own: configure an instance exactly the way you want, then run create-image against it to capture its current disk state as a new, reusable AMI. Launching ten identical application servers from one custom AMI is how you make sure they're actually identical.

Every instance reports one of a small set of states. Pending means it's being provisioned and isn't ready yet. Running means it's up and billing for compute. Stopping and stopped mean a shutdown was requested and completed — compute billing stops, but the root volume still exists. Shutting-down and terminated mean the instance is being, or has been, permanently torn down. describe-instances shows you exactly which state an instance is in right now.

This is the distinction that costs people data if they get it backwards. stop-instances powers the instance off but preserves the root EBS volume, so you can start it again later with everything exactly as you left it — only instance store volumes, if any, get wiped. terminate-instances deletes the instance permanently, and by default deletes the root volume with it, because DeleteOnTermination defaults to true unless you set it to false first.

The practical rule: stop an instance if you might need it again, terminate it only when you're certain you're done — and check that DeleteOnTermination flag first if the root disk actually matters.
